title: Email support is dead, long live support by email!
summary: Spam, AI agents, and auto-responder loops pushed Mux to move ticket creation to a web form. Here’s what changed, why, and how to reach our support team now.
body_markdown:
Published on


November 19, 2026


# Email support is dead, long live support by email!


By[Ben Chuba](https://www.mux.com/team/ben-chuba) • 5 min read •[Company](https://www.mux.com/blog/category/company)


---


Sometimes, when it feels like you have an out there idea, the more you think and talk about things, the more clear it becomes that the idea isn’t out there at all. That’s the sort of process that led Mux, on the 1st of November 2026, to make the long debated decision to disable the ability to create tickets via email. But what does that actually mean in practice? Simply put: going forward ticket **creation** happens via our handy webform at[mux.com/support](https://www.mux.com/support) , and ticket **communication** continues via the same trusty help@


email address. Let’s talk about why.


## Why kill email ingestion?


In a word: spam. While we’re certainly no strangers to cleaning up the occasional email blasts, or requests from our “CEO” for Apple gift cards (I’m lucky my local pharmacy is within walking distance!): two major spam-adjacent events have driven up the need for this ingestion/communication split.


### Muse, Dots, and Grok Bot, oh my!


The recent rise in dedicated personal agentic AI has also led to an increase in well-tailored, convincing, and directed spam or phishing attempts. Muse hit 10 million users within one month of launch, and specifically advertises handling emails for you in their marketing. Even on legitimate requests, interacting with agents tends to be fairly effort-intensive. We’d rather they find our[docs for agents](https://www.mux.com/docs/core/llms-txt) first and foremost, leaving only the unanswered questions for their human counterparts (or our support team) to field.


Meta advertises email as a key feature of their new Muse agent.


### The Support@ “Ticket Apocalypse”


On July 20, 2026, a rogue individual exposed a significant flaw in email etiquette and CC’ed together hundreds of support@


email addresses (a respectful BCC would be appreciated for future phishing scams, thank you very much!). Each support auto-responder created new tickets with us, to which we auto-responded, creating tickets with them. You can probably see where this is going, and regularly deleting 2000+ tickets isn’t where we want to be allocating our time.


There are some clever ways around this, specifically if the systems involved support[RFC 3834](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3834) , but we can’t count on that to be the case, and that’s speaking from experience: the 20th is just the worst this ever got, but it’s far from the only occurrence since.


See if you can figure out which day is July 20th!


## What effect did this have on tickets?


Since making this change, we’ve been keeping a close eye on the emails that we’re receiving. The numbers bear out the need to make this change:


- 73 percent of incoming emails were pure spam, phishing, or script injection attempts
- Of the 27 percent that were legitimate, 78 percent of email senders went on to open a ticket through Mux’s support form
- Incoming ticket counts have remained in line with historical baseline values


Additionally, one message immediately tested the limits of the new system: another case of an individual CC’ing together hundreds of support@


email addresses (this time a job application — they didn’t get the job). This email came in during off-hours, when our staff would not have been available to triage and get the situation under control as we had been able to previously. Under the previous system, this would have meant a ticket loop running unattended for hours. Now, these issues are dealt with swiftly and automatically, without any worry or input from our team.


Email us these days, and here’s what you’ll see.


## Extra credit


Of course, cutting down on spam isn’t all that we get out of directing developers to use our form for support rather than email. Having full control over the circumstances surrounding ticket submission allows us to collect and funnel additional information to our team, leading to better support experiences end to end. A user with a question about generating JWT tokens for Mux’s[DRM features](https://www.mux.com/docs/guides/protect-videos-with-drm) , may have context in their head that wouldn’t get relayed properly in pure text, but through our support form, we can ask them to pre-classify their ticket by category.


Collecting this information also gives our automated Docs Agent crucial context, leading to better results when a developer needs an instant answer, or our team isn’t in the office.


Talk to our Docs Agent, we promise they don’t bite!


## Can I still open a ticket without an account?


Yes! The last thing we wanted to do with this change is to put up a barrier to ticket creation that would lock out prospective developers, people having account access issues, etc.


While submitting a ticket from your actual account still gives our team the best context for answering your question, we definitely recognize that many questions need to be answered without an account.


Submitting a ticket is as easy as clicking this[link](https://www.mux.com/support) !


While the age of guessing a company’s support email address and firing off a quick request may be ending, Mux’s commitment to fast, quality, and personable customer support never will. Disabling email-based ticket creation allows our team at Mux to deliver even better support to you and your team, so if you’ve been waiting to reach out,[we’d love to hear from you](https://www.mux.com/support) , there’s never been a better time.
